theme: The LORD is my rock and my fortress
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 18:1-30. This is David’s great song of deliverance. Today read the first half, with its images of rescue and its confession of who God is.
settingTheScene: The title says David spoke this song “to the LORD on the day when the LORD rescued him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul.” It is also found, with small changes, in 2 Samuel 22, which you will read soon. Psalm 18 looks back on all of David’s flight and sums up what he learned. It stands here at the end of the years of fleeing, as David’s own testimony.
observation: “I love you, O LORD, my strength” (v. 1).
“The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold” (v. 2).
“The cords of death encompassed me; the torrents of destruction assailed me” (v. 4).
“In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I cried for help. From his temple he heard my voice” (v. 6).
“Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations also of the mountains trembled” (v. 7).
“He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the wind” (v. 10).
“He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters” (v. 16).
“He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me” (v. 19).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with love: “I love you, O LORD.” It is not an argument or a doctrine. It is an expression of the heart. And then David piles up images, seven of them in one verse: rock, fortress, deliverer, refuge, shield, horn of salvation, stronghold. He has been in caves and on cliffs, and he knows what a rock is. But he says that God is the true rock.

Then he describes the danger. The cords of death were around him. The torrents of destruction rushed at him. He was close to dying. And in that place, “I called upon the LORD.” This is the pattern of the whole Psalter: crying out, and being heard.

The description of God’s response is a spectacular poem. The earth shakes, smoke rises from his nostrils, he parts the heavens and comes down. The language is that of a storm and an earthquake, the imagery of the exodus and of Sinai. God comes to rescue one man in a cave. David is saying that the God of Sinai is the God who hears one frightened servant. His power is not remote but personal.

The rescue is described tenderly: “He drew me out of many waters.” The word for “drew” is the same as the one used for Moses (Exodus 2:10). “He brought me out into a broad place.” After years in narrow caves, David is brought to a spacious place. Why? “Because he delighted in me.” Behind the whole rescue is God’s delight in his servant. It is grace.

In verses 20 to 30, David speaks of his own righteousness. This must be read in context. He is not claiming sinlessness before God, but declaring that in the matter of his conflict with Saul, he has kept faith. And he rests on the principle that “with the merciful you show yourself merciful.” The final line of today’s reading is a famous one: “This God, his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.”
connection: Jesus is the ultimate rescued one. He was in the “cords of death,” and God raised him (Acts 2:24). Paul quotes verse 49 in Romans 15:9. Zechariah calls Christ “a horn of salvation” in Luke 1:69. Colossians 1:13 says that God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness.” And Psalm 18:2’s rock is Christ himself (1 Corinthians 10:4).
application:
Begin your prayer today with “I love you, O LORD.” Mean it.

Write down a time God brought you into a “broad place” after a narrow one.

Read verse 30 slowly: “His way is perfect.” Where do you struggle to believe it?
prayerPrompts: Tell God you love him, and say why.
Thank him for drawing you out of many waters.
Ask him to teach you to take refuge in him.
